item.title: Amazon and Intel headline the earnings releases after today’s close
item.description:
As the major indices trade modestly to sharply lower with the Nasdaq Composite (-1.59%) and the Nasdaq 100 (-1.66%) leading the downward spiral, some other big names will report after the close including Amazon and Intel. 

The central question for technology investors: Is the growth coming from AI strong enough to justify the spending—and support future profits and cash flow?

Consensus estimates vary slightly by provider. The comparisons below use current MarketBeat estimates against the same quarter a year ago; EPS generally reflects the adjusted measure used by analysts, except Amazon’s reported earnings.

Amazon: AWS growth and the cost of delivering it

  • EPS expected: $1.97 versus $1.95 a year ago—up approximately 1%.
  • Revenue expected: $202.21 billion versus $180.17 billion—up 12.2%.
  • Conference call: 5:00 PM ET.

A year ago, the stock was trading at around $225. It is currently trading at $244.71. 

The most important number could be Amazon Web Services revenue, with expectations around $45.4 billion–$45.6 billion, compared with approximately $33.0 billion a year ago. That implies growth of roughly 38%, a substantial acceleration from the 20% growth reported in last year’s third quarter. Investors will also examine AWS operating margins to judge how effectively that growth translates into profits.

The other major focus is Amazon’s approximately $220 billion capital-spending outlook. Strong cloud demand would be encouraging, but another increase in spending could keep attention on free cash flow. Holiday-quarter retail guidance, advertising growth and fulfillment profitability will also help shape the reaction.

An important earnings comparison: Last year’s $1.95 EPS included a $9.5 billion pretax gain from Amazon’s Anthropic investments. Consequently, the roughly flat headline EPS forecast does not provide a clean measure of underlying operating growth. Operating income, segment margins and cash flow deserve particular attention.

Intel: A stronger recovery is already expected

  • Adjusted EPS expected: approximately $0.41 versus $0.23—up roughly 77%, using the unrounded estimate.
  • Revenue expected: $16.54 billion versus $13.65 billion—up 21.1%.
  • Conference call: 5:00 PM ET.

Intel’s expectations already anticipate a meaningful improvement. Its own guidance called for $15.8 billion–$16.8 billion in revenue and adjusted EPS of $0.38, putting consensus above the revenue midpoint and above its earnings forecast. Intel Corporation

Investors will want evidence that demand for server processors can sustain the recovery, alongside updates on manufacturing capacity, margins and outside foundry customers. The next-quarter outlook and concrete progress in the foundry business may carry more weight than a modest earnings beat.

A year ago the stock was trading at $37

Other notable releases:

Starbucks: Improving profits despite lower reported revenue

  • Adjusted EPS expected: approximately $0.72 versus $0.52—up 38%.
  • Revenue expected: $9.22 billion versus $9.57 billion—down approximately 3.6%.
  • Conference call: 4:15 PM ET.

The revenue decline needs context: Starbucks’ conversion of its China operations to a licensed joint venture reduces consolidated sales, making the headline comparison less representative of customer demand.

The better barometers are U.S. comparable-store sales, transaction growth and operating margins. Management previously targeted U.S. comparable-sales growth of at least 6.5% for the quarter. Investors will also look closely at fiscal 2027 guidance to assess whether the turnaround can sustain its momentum.

  • Gilead Sciences: EPS expected at $2.19 versus $2.47, down 11.3%; revenue of $7.80 billion versus $7.77 billion, up 0.4%. The key question is whether guidance points toward improving profitability against a largely flat revenue comparison. marketbeat.com
  • First Solar: EPS expected at $4.67 versus $4.24, up 10.1%; revenue of $1.29 billion versus $1.59 billion, down approximately 19%. That divergence makes the explanation for stronger earnings, shipment timing and the forward outlook particularly relevant. marketbeat.com

For the technical setup, the distinction is between delivering growth and exceeding what the market has already priced in. Amazon faces elevated cloud expectations, while Intel is already expected to show a substantial recovery. The charts can help define whether buyers retain control going into those results—and where a disappointing reaction would put that control at risk.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: USDCHF tests key support as sellers challenge the 200-hour moving average
item.description:
The USDCHF is trading near session lows after breaking below its 100-hour moving average at 0.82758. That break gave sellers the technical go-ahead to push lower, with the decline extending to 0.8257, right at the 200-hour moving average. The price has since edged back to around 0.8262, leaving traders with a clearly defined battle between buyers and sellers.

The distinction between those two moving averages is important. The break below the 100-hour moving average shifted the near-term bias toward the sellers. However, reaching the 200-hour moving average introduces another decision point. Sellers have reached a downside target. To strengthen their control, they now need to break below that target and stay below it.

For buyers, the same level offers an opportunity to define and limit risk.

The buyer’s perspective: Define risk before entry

Why would a buyer step in when the price is falling? Because a technical trade does not require certainty that the market has bottomed. It requires a reason to enter, a clear point at which the trade idea is wrong, and enough potential reward to justify the risk.

A buyer leaning against the 200-hour moving average near 0.8257 is looking for that level to attract support. If the price holds above it and begins to recover, the buyer benefits from entering close to support. If the price breaks below and selling gathers momentum, the reason for the trade weakens, giving the buyer a nearby reference point for exiting.

That is an important trading lesson: the moving average does not guarantee a bounce. It provides a level around which a trader can build a plan. Risk can be defined before entry, limited through an exit strategy, and accepted as part of the trade.

The seller’s perspective: Turn an opinion into a technical plan

The bearish trader can use that same moving average from the opposite perspective.

If you expect the USDCHF to continue lower, the 200-hour moving average becomes a level the price needs to get to, get through, and stay below. A bearish opinion alone does not confirm that sellers are in control. The price action around support provides evidence of whether other traders agree.

A sustained break below 0.8257, followed by an inability to reclaim the moving average, would suggest buyers are losing that battle. If a subsequent rebound stalls against the moving average from below, former support could become resistance. That would give sellers another reference point for managing risk.

Conversely, a brief dip below the moving average followed by a quick recovery would raise the possibility of a failed break. Sellers looking for downside follow-through could become vulnerable if the market cannot remain below support.

Downside targets: What comes after a break?

On a sustained break lower, the next downside target comes at the 38.2% retracement at 0.8224. That level sits near the upper boundary of a swing area extending down to 0.82162.

Together, those levels form another support zone where traders would assess whether the selling can continue. Reaching the zone would satisfy another downside objective. Breaking through it—and staying below—would strengthen the bearish case further.

A break below that zone would open the door toward last week’s low at 0.81905.

The recovery scenario: What buyers need to reclaim

If the 200-hour moving average holds, buyers would first look for a recovery toward the 100-hour moving average at 0.82758.

Holding support would be an initial positive, but reclaiming that higher moving average would provide stronger evidence that buyers are regaining control. The move would also call into question the earlier downside break, increasing the potential for sellers to cover positions.

Staying above the 100-hour moving average would put yesterday’s high at 0.8312 back in focus.

The key lesson: Let the price action guide the trade

For now, 0.8257 is the key barometer. Buyers can use it to define risk on a support trade. Sellers need a sustained break below it to reinforce the bearish bias.

The value of the technical level is that it gives both sides a reference point. Traders can measure whether the market is supporting their position and identify when the evidence changes.

Have an opinion, but build the trade around a level that defines your risk. Then let the price action determine whether the trade deserves to stay open.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Trump: Iran war will be over very soon. Senator warns of 'insane' US plans
item.description:
Trump has said this at least 100 times since the war started in late February. He is an improviser, not a planner. Since it all went sideways, he has been looking for an elegant exit but can't find one. The blockade may be giving him some leverage but the pain of higher oil prices is making it an extremely unpopular war.

Meanwhile, the UKMTO reports that a tanker has been struck by an unknown projectile whilst completing an outbound transit of the Strait of Hormuz. There are no reported injuries to the crew or environmental impact report at this time.

The status quo can't continue indefinitely so it will either be escalation or negotiation. It looks like the US will now wait until after the midterms to attack, though some are speculating later in November when another aircraft carrier arrives.

Oil product prices remain at sky high levels while crude oil is down 79 cents to $101.98 today.

Here is an ominous message from Connecticut Senator Chris Murphy (D), who is also a member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and sits on the defense appropriations subcommittee:

Trump is reportedly planning to restart war with Iran after the election. Some of us have been briefed on the war plan. And while I cannot disclose any details, I can say this: the plan is insane. It will not achieve objectives and will set off a new cycle of escalation.

That's certainly ominous. He went onto say that it would undermine the US commitment to rule of law and would include attacks on civilian infrastructure.

"I will just say this - their plan is insane ...it will lead to devastating escalation and the likely destruction of our commitment to the rule of law. There has been open reporting as to the civilian infrastructure we may be targeting…. I think the plan they have developed will lead in my view to a prolongment and escalation of this war that will be devastating to our security interests"

The leaks suggest attacks on:

  • Electricity generation and transmission facilities

  • Bridges and transportation networks

  • Oil refineries and energy infrastructure

  • Potentially other infrastructure essential to civilian life

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Iran's Ghalibaf: Progress can only be achieved once the seven conditions have been agreed upon
item.description:
Iran this week has repeated its 'seven conditions' several times and most of it was part of the agreement with the US from June 17.

Here is a recap:

1. End military operations on all fronts. A permanent halt to attacks against Iran and allied groups, including in Lebanon, Yemen, Iraq and the Palestinian territories.

2. Release frozen Iranian assets. Unfreeze Iranian money held overseas, with approximately $12 billion identified in subsequent negotiations.

3. Lift the US naval blockade. End restrictions on Iranian ports, tankers and commercial shipping.

4. Remove economic and political sanctions. Restore Iran's ability to export oil and conduct international financial transactions.

5. Withdraw US naval and air forces from the region. End the American military deployments and operations that Tehran regards as threatening Iran.

6. Pay war reparations. Compensate Iran for damage inflicted during the 2025 and 2026 conflicts.

7. End threats and hostile interference. Stop military threats, hostile rhetoric and what Tehran considers interference in its internal affairs.

The US is demanding action on the nuclear to file to go along with whatever it's prepared to do in terms of those conditions. For me, this doesn't sound like Iran is particularly worried about fresh US strikes but everyone talks tough before going to the negotiating table.

WTI crude oil was last down $1.17 to $101.60.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: WTI crude oil rebounds after a failed break below $100 and the 200-hour MA
item.description:
WTI crude oil had traded above its 200-hour moving average since breaking higher on October 12. Today, that support finally cracked. The price fell below the rising 200-hour moving average at $100.08 and the psychologically important $100 level, reaching a session low of $99.79.

Those breaks gave sellers two reasons to push lower. However, the follow-through was limited. The decline stalled ahead of Tuesday’s low at $99.45, and the price rebounded back above both $100 and the 200-hour moving average.

Crude is now trading near $101.05, leaving it between the 200-hour moving average at $100.08 and the 100-hour moving average at $101.48. Those two levels frame the next battle between buyers and sellers.

The failed break below support disappointed sellers, but buyers still have work to do. A crack in a level that has held for an extended period can change traders’ mindset. Buyers who previously leaned confidently against the 200-hour moving average have now seen that support give way—even if only briefly.

To regain more control, buyers need to push the price above $101.48 and stay above it. That would strengthen the recovery and suggest today’s downside break was a failed attempt to shift control to the sellers.

Conversely, a move back below $100.08 and $100 would put sellers back in position to test $99.79, followed by the more important $99.45 low. Breaking that Tuesday low would add confirmation to the bearish move.

Until the price breaks free, the two hourly moving averages remain the key barometers. Watch for a sustained break and follow-through momentum. Today’s reversal is a reminder that getting through a technical level is only the first step. Staying through it is what gives traders greater confidence in the move.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Boeing stock analysis: Is the earnings selloff a buy-the-dip opportunity?
item.description:
Boeing stock rebounds after a 10.7% earnings plunge. Is the next dip worth buying?

Boeing shares are recovering from a sharp selloff, but the next pullback could tell investors more than the rebound itself. Here's why the $169-$171 area matters, what could support a longer-term recovery and how a hypothetical position might manage the risk.

Boeing (NYSE: BA) is showing signs of recovery after a painful post-earnings selloff. But is this the beginning of a longer-term buying opportunity or just a temporary rebound? I'm particularly interested in whether buyers can defend the $169-$171 area on the next pullback, rather than simply chasing the stock higher.

As of approximately 11:50 a.m. New York time on October 29, Boeing shares were trading around $173.60, up approximately 3.9% from Wednesday's close, based on delayed intraday data.

That's an encouraging recovery, but it follows a substantial decline.

Boeing shares plunged 10.7% on October 27, closing at $168.18 after trading at $188.31 immediately before earnings. The selling continued on October 28, when shares reached $165.01 before closing at $167.14.

The question now is whether the market has sufficiently adjusted to the earnings disappointment, or whether sellers will return when the initial enthusiasm fades.

Boeing's earnings weren't all bad. So why did the stock plunge?

Boeing's third-quarter earnings report contained several positive developments.

Revenue reached $24.2 billion, up 4% year over year. The company generated approximately $464 million in quarterly free cash flow, reported a record $745 billion backlog and continued to make progress on important aircraft certification programs.

The FAA's recent certification of Boeing's 737 MAX 10 was another meaningful milestone, opening the way for deliveries of an aircraft with substantial existing orders.

But there is a difference between having strong demand and converting that demand into profitable aircraft deliveries.

That distinction helps explain the negative market reaction.

As Reuters reported, Boeing's progress toward producing 47 737 aircraft per month has been slower than anticipated, with that production milestone now expected in early 2027.

The company also outlined approximately $3 billion in expected free cash flow for 2027, below the $5.5 billion analyst consensus cited by Reuters. Its $10 billion annual free-cash-flow ambition has shifted to 2029.

There's another important number investors should monitor.

Despite generating positive free cash flow in the third quarter, Boeing's cumulative free cash flow for the first nine months of 2026 remained negative at approximately $359 million.

To achieve its roughly $2 billion full-year free-cash-flow expectation, Boeing would therefore need to generate approximately $2.36 billion in the fourth quarter.

That's a substantial amount of cash generation still to deliver.

The company's backlog provides potential future revenue, but execution, production efficiency and cash conversion will determine how much value eventually reaches shareholders.

The next Boeing stock pullback could be more revealing than today's rally

For a possible longer-term buy-the-dip opportunity, I would focus on a few specific price areas.

$169-$171: The first area I want buyers to defend

This is perhaps the most interesting near-term support candidate.

Boeing struggled to sustain a recovery above this region immediately following its earnings selloff. Thursday's rally has now carried shares beyond it.

What happens if the stock returns?

If Boeing pulls back toward $169-$171, briefly slips below part of that area but recovers, and then establishes a higher low, I would view that as potentially constructive.

It would suggest buyers are becoming more willing to defend prices that previously presented difficulties.

The important point is not merely touching $170. It is how the stock behaves around that price and whether buying interest persists after the initial rebound.

A successful defense during broader stock-market weakness would be particularly interesting, although not conclusive.

$165-$167: A deeper test of whether a bottom is developing

Wednesday's low of $165.01 provides a useful reference.

If Boeing revisits this area, buyers would have another opportunity to demonstrate that selling pressure is weakening.

Even a temporary move below $165 followed by a convincing recovery could still be consistent with a developing bottom.

However, sustained trading beneath the area, particularly if attempted recoveries repeatedly fail, would weaken the bullish interpretation.

$174-$176 and $178-$179: Recovery checkpoints

On the upside, $174-$176 represents the first nearby area to monitor.

Beyond that, $178-$179 is a more meaningful recovery checkpoint.

A move above these areas, followed by an ability to hold them during subsequent pullbacks, would strengthen the case that the recovery is becoming more durable.

A sustained improvement could eventually bring the $188-$190 region back into view, near Boeing's pre-earnings trading prices.

None of these outcomes is guaranteed. They are observable tests that can help investors assess whether a rebound is developing into something more substantial.

An educational Boeing buy-the-dip strategy for longer-term investors

One lesson I find useful when considering a stock following a sharp decline is that a good-looking price and a good entry are not necessarily the same thing.

An investor might like Boeing at $169.50, but a return to that price alone would not establish that the stock is ready to recover.

For illustration, consider a hypothetical strategy that waits for a pullback into the $168-$171 region, followed by evidence of stabilization and renewed buying.

The following example assumes an entry at $169.50. It is not a recommendation to buy at that price, and no future entry or execution is assumed.

Conditional entry: $169.50

Only after a qualifying pullback and signs that buyers are defending the area. The price may never return there, or the necessary confirmation may develop at a different price.

Protective stop: $157.50

This places the initial exit level beneath the recent $165.01 low and the deeper $160 reference area. It provides more room for volatility than a tight short-term stop but exposes the investor to a larger potential loss.

Initial risk: $12 per share, approximately 7.1%

The risk calculation assumes execution at the stated entry and stop, before costs, slippage or price gaps.

First profit target: $188

Potential reward of $18.50 per share, or approximately 1.54 times the initial risk.

Second profit target: $210

Potential reward of $40.50 per share, or approximately 3.38 times the initial risk.

Third profit target: $235

Potential reward of $65.50 per share, or approximately 5.46 times the initial risk.

Intended holding period: 6-12 months

The targets are illustrative recovery milestones, not forecasts or estimates of the probability that Boeing will reach them.

An investor could consider selling one-third of the original position at each target.

Another optional approach would be to move the protective stop on the remaining shares to the original entry price after the first profit target is reached.

That could reduce the remaining position's exposure to an ordinary price reversal, although a subsequent pullback could also stop out the remaining shares before a larger recovery.

Importantly, a stop at the entry price does not guarantee a breakeven exit. Gaps, slippage and trading costs can affect actual results.

And the 1.54, 3.38 and 5.46 reward-to-risk figures describe individual targets relative to the original risk, not the expected profitability of the overall strategy.

What could go wrong with a Boeing buy-the-dip investment?

There are two separate risks to consider.

The first is price action.

A strong rebound immediately after a large decline can sometimes attract buyers without representing a sustainable change in direction.

If Boeing cannot maintain the $169-$171 area, falls below $165 and repeatedly fails to recover, the argument for an emerging bottom would deteriorate.

The second risk is fundamental.

Boeing is still working through a complicated operational recovery. Production targets, supply-chain constraints, aircraft deliveries, manufacturing quality and free-cash-flow generation remain important uncertainties.

Even if the company makes genuine progress, its shares could struggle if actual results fall short of expectations.

And a stock recovering technically does not automatically mean its valuation is attractive for a six-to-twelve-month investment.

Investors should also weigh Boeing's debt, prospective earnings and cash flow against the price they are being asked to pay.

An alternative is simply to wait.

An investor seeking greater confirmation could allow Boeing to reclaim $178-$179, or even demonstrate a more sustained recovery toward its pre-earnings prices.

That might mean paying more for the shares, but potentially with stronger evidence that the immediate selling pressure has diminished.

Waiting for confirmation has its own trade-offs, but there is no requirement to participate in every potential bottom.

My bottom line on Boeing stock

I find Boeing interesting after its substantial earnings-related decline, particularly because the company's long-term demand picture has not disappeared.

But the market has also received genuine reasons to question the speed and profitability of its turnaround.

For now, the $169-$171 area is the first price region I would watch carefully.

If buyers defend it, establish a higher low and eventually overcome the next recovery checkpoints, the case for a longer-term position could improve.

If those defenses fail, there may be a better opportunity later, or no opportunity worth taking under the current assumptions.

The objective isn't to predict Boeing's exact bottom. It's to identify what the stock needs to demonstrate before putting capital at risk.

Educational only. Trade at your own risk. The hypothetical strategy is not personalized investment advice. Prices, levels and conditions should be reassessed against current market data before any investment decision.

This article was written by Itai Levitan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold slips below its 100-hour MA as interest-rate concerns weigh on the recovery
item.description:
Fundamentally, and the recent him broader view, gold’s retreat from its August high reflects a market more concerned about higher interest rates than attracted to its protection against inflation and geopolitical uncertainty. Higher Treasury yields, a firm dollar and expectations of further Federal Reserve tightening have made it difficult for buyers to sustain a recovery.

That highlights an important distinction for gold traders. Although gold is often viewed as an inflation hedge, higher inflation does not automatically translate into higher gold prices. If inflation leads investors to expect tighter monetary policy and higher yields, the interest-rate response can outweigh demand for inflation protection. Gold pays no interest, so higher yields increase the opportunity cost of holding the metal. A stronger dollar can add another headwind by making dollar-denominated gold more expensive for buyers using other currencies.

Spot gold fell to $3,975 last Friday, its lowest level since mid-July, before recovering above the psychologically important $4,000 level early this week. Lower oil prices helped ease inflation concerns, offering some relief from the pressure surrounding the interest-rate outlook. However, that rebound has struggled to develop into a more convincing recovery.

The Fed’s decision to hold rates unchanged yesterday did little to remove that headwind. Attention has already shifted toward December, with the market pricing in approximately an 84% probability of a rate increase, according to the pricing cited. A pause in October therefore does not necessarily signal an end to the tightening cycle. As long as another hike remains heavily priced, gold buyers face a difficult backdrop.

That does not prevent corrective rallies. It does, however, put greater importance on whether those rallies can clear technical resistance and hold above it.

Wednesday’s recovery stalled at a key technical barometer

Technically, buyers pushed gold toward $4,080 on Wednesday, but the advance stalled near the falling 200-hour moving average. Sellers leaned against that resistance and pushed the price back to the downside.

The location of that reversal matters. A recovery toward a widely watched moving average gives buyers an opportunity to demonstrate greater control. When the price fails to break above that level, sellers have a defined area against which to limit risk. Wednesday’s rejection left the recovery incomplete and reinforced the importance of the 200-hour moving average as an overhead barometer.

Until buyers can move above—and stay above—that moving average, sellers retain an important technical advantage.

The 100-hour MA is the immediate battleground

In trading today, gold has extended below its 100-hour moving average at $4,026.50 (blue line on the chart above). The price is trading near $4,025, down approximately $41, or 1.03%, leaving it just below that technical level.

Lower Treasury yields today have offered some support and helped slow the decline. Nevertheless, buyers still need to turn that support into a sustained move back above the 100-hour moving average.

For traders, the distinction is between a brief break and acceptance below the level. A quick recovery above $4,026.50 would suggest the downside break is failing, giving buyers an initial foothold. Holding above it would then bring attention back toward Wednesday’s high near $4,080 and the falling 200-hour moving average.

Conversely, if rebounds stall at or below the 100-hour moving average, the former support would begin acting as resistance. That would keep sellers in control of the immediate bias.

A sustained break lower would expose the October low

On the downside, $4,000 is the next psychological reference point, followed by the October low at $3,975.40. A break below that low would extend the decline and expose the broader swing area between $3,942.71 and $3,959.37, defined by lows going back to June and July.

That swing area would become an important test of whether buyers are willing to defend longer-standing support. Buyers leaning against it would have a defined risk level below the zone. A sustained break beneath it would weaken the broader technical picture further.

For now, $4,026.50 is the close-risk barometer. Below it, sellers retain the immediate advantage, with $4,000 and $3,975.40 in focus. Above it, buyers can begin repairing today’s technical damage—but clearing the falling 200-hour moving average remains the more significant hurdle.

Gold technical ladder: the levels defining the next move

The 100-hour moving average at $4,026.50 is the immediate barometer for buyers and sellers. Holding below it keeps the near-term bias tilted lower, while a sustained recovery above would give buyers an initial foothold.

On the topside, the next key hurdle is the $4,080 area, where Wednesday’s rally stalled near the falling 200-hour moving average. Buyers need to clear that resistance to strengthen the recovery.

Below the market, $4,000 provides a psychological reference point ahead of the October low at $3,975.40. A break below that low would expose the broader $3,942.71–$3,959.37 swing area, defined by lows from June and July.

The ladder provides a framework for managing risk: watch whether price breaks a level and holds beyond it, or fails and reverses. A failed break can be just as revealing as a sustained breakout, particularly when buyers and sellers are battling around a widely followed moving average.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: The door remains ajar for ECB to tighten. EURUSD rebounds after break lower failed
item.description:
The ECB kept interest rates unchanged as expected, but President Christine Lagarde delivered a hawkish message despite the decision to hold. Policymakers discussed a rate increase, and Lagarde indicated that conditions could have justified additional tightening. The decision to wait reflected unchanged underlying inflation and uncertainty surrounding the outlook, rather than a declaration that the tightening cycle was over.

For EURUSD, the decision and press conference produced volatile trading. An initial decline took the price below the double bottom near 1.11135, established on October 14 and revisited yesterday. However, sellers could not sustain the break. After reaching 1.1106, the pair reversed higher and rebounded toward 1.1155.

That recovery brought the price into a familiar swing area, with the falling 100-hour moving average just above. The failed break lower gives buyers an opportunity, but getting through resistance is the next requirement.

A hawkish hold keeps the next meeting in focus

Lagarde stressed that holding rates at this meeting does not rule out an increase at the next. Underlying inflation remains a key policy barometer, while elevated energy prices and geopolitical developments continue to complicate the outlook.

The distinction matters. A central bank can leave rates unchanged while still delivering a hawkish message if its guidance keeps further tightening in play. Markets respond to changes in the expected path of rates, as well as the decision announced that day.

Underlying inflation helps policymakers assess how persistent price pressures are beneath volatile headline components. Higher energy costs can lift headline inflation directly, but the broader concern is whether those increases feed into other prices, wages and inflation expectations.

The ECB’s message leaves room to gather more evidence while retaining the option to act.

Incoming data will shape the next decision

On growth, the ECB will assess incoming GDP figures alongside wages, unemployment and November PMIs to judge how the economy is absorbing tighter financing conditions. Updated staff projections and two additional inflation reports will also help shape the next decision.

Those releases matter because monetary policy works with a lag. Higher borrowing costs gradually influence household spending, business investment and demand. Policymakers must judge whether that restraint is sufficient to bring inflation down, or whether persistent price pressures require another increase.

For traders, this keeps the focus on how the data change expectations. Persistent inflation alongside resilient activity could strengthen the case for further tightening. Softer inflation and weaker growth could support another period of waiting.

The break below 1.11135 fails to attract follow-through

Technically, the initial move below 1.11135 gave sellers an opportunity to extend the decline (see chart above). That level had attracted buyers twice, making it an identifiable floor and a logical downside barometer.

However, the move to 1.1106 quickly reversed.

A support break needs follow-through to reinforce the bearish signal. When the price moves below a well-defined floor and then quickly recovers above it, the failure can encourage short covering and fresh buying. Traders who sold the break may find themselves holding positions below a reclaimed support level.

That does not automatically establish a lasting bottom. It does show that sellers failed to maintain control below the old floor. Buyers now need to build on that rejection by breaking resistance above.

Buyers face resistance at 1.1152–1.11616

The rebound toward 1.1155 carried EURUSD into the swing area between 1.1152 and 1.11602. Just above that zone sits the falling 100-hour moving average at 1.11616.

Together, those levels create the first important resistance hurdle.

item.title: Why markets often move in the opposite direction to the news?
item.description:
One of the most confusing aspects of financial markets for new traders is that prices often move in the opposite direction to what the news suggest. Stocks can fall after strong economic data, gold can fall despite geopolitical tensions, and bonds can rise following an inflation surprise. The most important thing to know is that markets react to how new information changes expectations, not whether the news is good or bad.

Financial markets are forward-looking. Prices reflect what traders collectively expect to happen over the coming months, meaning much of the anticipated impact of an economic release or policy decision may be already priced in. 

What matters the most is how the actual outcome compares to what the market expected. For example, if markets expect the Federal Reserve to signal two more rate hikes, the US dollar could still fall if the central bank delivers on expectations, simply because the outcome was already expected. If the Fed, on the other hand, signals more rate hikes than expected, the greenback can rally hard as markets reprice expectations.

Ever heard the term "good news is bad news"? Well, economic data can affect multiple variables simultaneously. Stronger growth, for instance, can support corporate earnings while increasing inflationary pressures and reducing the likelihood of monetary easing.

Suppose US economic activity accelerates unexpectedly. Depending on the economic context, this development can lead to higher interest rate expectations which could eventually slow growth and therefore push the stock market lower. So, the stock market would react based on expectations about the future economic outlook and not on the current one. 

Another important factor is positioning. When a trade becomes too crowded, even a relatively small change in the outlook can trigger a significant reversal as traders take profits or rush to uwind their positions.

For example, if traders are heavily positioned for dollar weakness ahead of a Federal Reserve meeting, a decision that is just less dovish than expected could trigger a sharp dollar rally. Traders could unwind bearish positions even if the Fed has not delivered an outright hawkish surprise on expectations that in the near-future the Fed could indeed turn more hawkish. This is why the magnitude of a market move isn't always related to the news. Positioning can play a very important role.

Remember that financial markets are in a continuous process of assessing and reassessing the future. Every new economic release, central bank comment or geopolitical development can change future expectations and trigger big moves.

Consider an unexpected increase in oil prices. Initially, traders may focus on the resulting inflationary pressures, pushing bond yields higher and increasing expectations for tighter monetary policy. If the shock persists, however, concerns about weaker consumption, slower growth and eventually monetary easing may become more important.

The dominant market narrative can therefore change over time, even when the underlying development remains the same. This also explains why an initial price reaction can reverse shortly after a major announcement. Traders (mostly algos) may first respond to the headline before reassessing the broader implications for the economy. 

In conclusion, the three key questions you should always ask yourself are:

  • What was already priced in?
  • How does the news change the expectations?
  • What could be the catalyst for a repricing?

The last question is often the most important one because markets can extend beyond the fundamentals. Such mispricings can create mean-reversion opportunities, but the timing is key because "markets can remain irrational longer than you can stay solvent".

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: US GDP Advance for the 3rd quarter 3.4% vs 3.2% estimate
item.description:
• Prior quarter 2,2%

The details 

  • GDP: 3.4% vs 3.2% expected. Prior revised to 2.2% from 1.5%.

  • Real final sales: 1.7% vs 2.0% expected. Prior 2.8%

  • Consumer spending: 3.8%. Prior 3.8%.

  • GDP deflator: 2.2% vs 3.5% expected. Prior 6.1%

  • Core PCE prices: 2.5% vs 2.4% expected. Prior 3.3%

  • PCE prices: 2.1% vs 2.6% expected. Prior 5.0%

What drove the GDP increase?

The 3.4% increase in Q3 GDP was supported by investment, consumer spending and government spending. Trade was the main drag, with exports falling and imports rising.

  • Investment was the largest positive contributor, adding 3.27% to growth. That category includes business investment, housing and changes in inventories.

  • Consumer spending added roughly 2.52%, reinforcing the importance of household demand to the expansion.

  • Government spending added 0.90%, providing another source of support.

  • Lower exports subtracted 0.68%, reflecting a decline in sales of US-produced goods and services abroad.

  • Higher imports subtracted 2.64%. Imports are deducted because GDP measures domestic production, while spending on imported products is included elsewhere in the accounts.

The takeaway is that domestic spending carried the economy while trade weighed heavily on growth. Investment was a major support, but the distinction between productive investment and inventory accumulation matters. With final sales growing more slowly than headline GDP, the sustainability of the inventory contribution will be something to watch.

From the BEA: Behind the GDP increase: inventories, computers and consumer spending

The BEA’s breakdown shows that inventory accumulation, computer equipment and consumer spending supported the 3.4% annualized increase in Q3 GDP, while trade weighed on growth.

  • Investment: Growth was driven primarily by inventories and equipment. Wholesale businesses and manufacturers increased inventories, led by nondurable goods. Equipment spending was supported by computers and peripheral equipment.

  • Consumer spending: Both services and goods increased. Health care, restaurant meals and accommodations led services spending, while prescription drugs were a major contributor to goods spending.

  • Government spending: Federal nondefense spending accounted for more than the overall increase. However, the BEA highlighted an accounting effect from smaller Strategic Petroleum Reserve oil sales compared with Q2. That lifted measured government consumption, but the BEA said those sales have no direct effect on overall GDP, because they are reflected elsewhere in the accounts.

  • Trade: Exports fell, led by petroleum and related products. Imports increased, with capital goods excluding autos the largest contributor (AI spending). Falling exports and rising imports both weighed on GDP.

The details show solid consumer demand and strength in computer equipment spending, but inventories also played an important role. That helps explain why headline GDP outpaced final sales and leaves a question for coming quarters: will businesses sustain production as those inventories are sold?

Overall Summary

The US economy grew at a 3.4% annualized pace in Q3, according to the advance GDP figures from the Bureau of Economic Analysis. That was above the 3.2% consensus estimate and slightly stronger than the Atlanta Fed’s final 3.3% GDPNow forecast. Consumer spending remained healthy, growing 3.8%, matching the preceding quarter.

The result supports Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh’s message at yesterday’s press conference that growth had strengthened. Warsh said first-half growth had been revised to 2.4% from 1.8%, with Q3 likely running above 3%, led by healthy consumer spending.

However, the details were more mixed than the headline. Real final sales grew just 1.7%, below expectations and down from 2.8% previously. Final sales exclude inventory changes, so that gap indicates inventory accumulation helped lift headline GDP. Inflation cooled sharply from Q2, although core PCE prices at 2.5% were slightly above the 2.4% estimate.

Quick analysis: Stronger growth, steady consumer spending and cooler inflation give the Fed some room to assess incoming data. The headline would normally support the dollar and Treasury yields, but weaker final sales and the softer broad inflation readings could temper that response. The key question is whether growth can sustain this pace without as much help from inventories.

What this report measures: Gross domestic product, or GDP, measures the value of goods and services produced in the United States. These quarterly growth figures are adjusted for inflation and expressed at annualized rates. The advance estimate is the first reading and is subject to revision.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.description:
The day after the Fed, markets have another set of questions to answer.

Did Chair Warsh give the economy more room to grow, or simply give the Fed more time before another rate hike? Are massive AI investments generating sufficient returns? And will today’s growth and inflation reports support the market’s expectations for additional tightening?

Treasury yields are lower across the curve, the dollar is modestly higher against some currencies and lower against others, and U.S. equity futures are under pressure. The Nasdaq is leading the decline as a sharp premarket fall in Alphabet overshadows stronger results from Microsoft.

Warsh’s message: Healthy growth, elevated inflation and time to assess

The Fed held its target range at 3.75%–4.00%, with a 10–2 vote. Warsh described an economy with healthy consumer spending, strong business investment and positive employment conditions. He indicated that third-quarter growth was likely above 3%. Inflation, however, remains too high, and renewed increases in energy prices raise the risk that price pressures could spread more broadly.

Warsh also suggested that September’s tightening is beginning to work. Some households and businesses face tighter credit conditions, although he stopped short of describing overall financial conditions as tight. His message was to gather more information before deciding the next step. Another hike remains possible, but he did not commit to a December move. See InvestingLive’s coverage of Warsh’s press conference.

For the economy, my takeaway is that the Fed sees enough strength to keep its attention on inflation. There was little indication of an urgent need to support growth through lower rates.

For markets, the distinction matters. A Fed willing to wait can provide some relief from immediate tightening concerns. But persistent inflation and healthy demand would keep borrowing costs elevated and make it harder to justify increasingly expensive equity valuations.

Yesterday’s reaction also showed that markets can interpret the same decision differently across maturities. From just before the announcement through the end of the press conference, the dollar fell, shorter-term yields declined and longer-term yields rose. That steepening showed that relief at the front end did not extend across the entire Treasury curve. This morning, longer-term yields are also moving lower.

Alphabet and Microsoft deliver contrasting AI messages

Alphabet is the main source of pressure on technology sentiment, with shares down more than 11% in premarket trading.

The company reported EPS of $2.12 versus $3.03 expected — MISS, and revenue of $127.6 billion versus $127.91 billion expected — MISS. Google Cloud was a bright spot, but Search and YouTube advertising revenue fell short of expectations.

The concern goes beyond the headline miss. Advertising revenue grew at its slowest pace in five quarters, while management said AI Mode searches were being monetized more slowly than traditional searches. At the same time, capital expenditures climbed to approximately $51.4 billion, up about $6.5 billion from the previous quarter, and free cash flow moved deeper into negative territory.

Investors are being asked to fund a substantial investment cycle while waiting for clearer evidence of the returns. Slower monetization makes that wait more uncomfortable.

Microsoft delivered a stronger message. Adjusted EPS of $4.89 BEAT expectations, while revenue of $92.28 billion also BEAT, increasing 19% from a year earlier. Azure growth of 48% offered evidence that demand for cloud and AI services continues to expand strongly.

Microsoft shares are higher in premarket trading (+1.5%), although that strength has not been enough to offset the broader technology weakness. The company’s reported buyout program—with roughly 60,000 employees potentially eligible—also puts efficiency and costs alongside growth in the discussion.

The broader lesson is that investors are becoming more selective. Spending on AI infrastructure needs to translate into revenue, margins and cash flow. Microsoft’s report provided more encouragement on that front. Alphabet’s raised more questions.

item.title: Alphabet stock plunged nearly 10% after hours. Why investors who don't own it should pay attention.
item.description:
Alphabet tumbles as Microsoft rises. Wall Street's earnings divide is becoming harder to ignore

Alphabet, ServiceNow and Fortinet suffered sharp after-hours selloffs, while Microsoft gained. The contrast raises an important question for stock investors: Are these isolated disappointments, or is Wall Street becoming less forgiving of companies that fail to meet increasingly demanding expectations?

Wall Street's earnings season has produced another warning for technology stock investors, but it is not simply that companies are reporting disappointing results.

Following the October 28 earnings announcements, Alphabet (GOOGL) fell nearly 10% in after-hours trading (see my latest post earnings GOOG stock analysis with what I'm watching), Microsoft (MSFT) gained, and ServiceNow (NOW) and Fortinet (FTNT) suffered even steeper declines.

The interesting part is that some of these companies reported substantial growth and, in certain cases, exceeded headline earnings expectations. Yet their shares were punished anyway.

My main takeaway is that investors should pay attention not only to earnings results, but also to how the market reacts to them, how those reactions compare with expectations, and whether the initial moves hold.

Six earnings reactions reveal a sharply divided market

The following figures come from an October 28, 2026 after-hours market snapshot, captured at approximately 9:35 p.m. New York time.

Source: Supplied October 28 earnings-reaction and options-implied movement snapshot. These are preliminary after-hours observations, not October 29 regular-session returns. Expected moves are indicative magnitudes, not guaranteed trading boundaries.

Three companies stand out.

Alphabet declined approximately 1.60 timesits expected move, ServiceNow 1.71 times, and Fortinet 2.19 times.

In other words, their initial selling pressure exceeded what options pricing had suggested was a typical earnings-event movement.

Microsoft offered an important counterexample. Its stock gained after reporting stronger revenue and profit growth, including fiscal first-quarter revenue of $92.3 billion, up 19% year over year.

Alphabet's results were more complicated. Revenue rose 25% to $127.6 billion and Google Cloud revenue surged 103%, but search advertising performance and approximately $9.1 billion of negative free cash flow raised concerns about the company's investment spending and future profitability.

These are not identical business stories. They are, however, examples of investors assigning very different values to growth, expectations and execution.

Fortinet's selloff reveals why beating earnings estimates is no longer enough

Fortinet offers perhaps the most instructive example.

The cybersecurity company reported quarterly revenue of $2.08 billion, up 20% year over year, while adjusted earnings reached $0.91 per share. Both exceeded Wall Street estimates.

Fortinet also raised its full-year revenue guidance. Yet its shares plunged by approximately 25% in the initial reaction.

Why?

Investors were looking beyond the headline figures. Service revenue missed expectations, and billings growth exceeded forecasts by a smaller margin than in the previous quarter. These details mattered particularly after a substantial rally in Fortinet shares ahead of earnings.

ServiceNow presented a similar disconnect between business performance and share-price performance.

The company reported subscription revenue growth of 21% and raised its full-year subscription revenue and free cash flow margin outlook. Nevertheless, the stock suffered a steep selloff, with investors also responding to weaker-than-expected earnings and near-term guidance concerns.

The lesson is that strong business growth and a positive stock-market reaction are two different things.

A company may perform well operationally but still disappoint investors who have already priced in even better results.

Earnings breadth is telling one story. The biggest stocks are telling another.

This is where the wider earnings picture becomes particularly interesting.

In my October 28 analysis of Wall Street's earnings recovery, I highlighted improving reactions across reporting companies, alongside a more concerning pattern among some of the largest stocks.

Earlier in earnings season, Netflix disappointed, while Meta and Tesla initially rallied after reporting but subsequently surrendered those gains.

There were encouraging developments afterward. On October 26, more than 70% of companies in the analyzed earnings cohort registered positive reactions, and October 27 also showed positive average performance.

But the new October 28 after-hours sample painted a much weaker picture.

Companies in sample

133

Positive reactions

34.6%

Capitalization-weighted reaction

-3.44%

Expected-move breaches

9 down / 4 up

Supplied October 28 after-hours sample. Provisional aggregate observations, not actual S&P 500 or Nasdaq returns. Aggregate calculations have not been independently reproduced.

Perhaps most revealing was the effect of individual technology giants on the capitalization-weighted sample.

Alphabet contributed approximately -4.04 percentage points to the sample's weighted reaction, while Microsoft's positive contribution was about +1.16 percentage points.

Why does that matter?

Because investors holding capitalization-weighted funds, including many S&P 500 and Nasdaq-linked ETFs, have much greater exposure to the largest companies than to smaller index constituents.

A market can therefore have improving earnings reactions across many businesses while a handful of influential stocks place significant pressure on investor portfolios.

The sample is not an index-performance calculation, but it illustrates an important distinction between how many stocks are doing well and how much influence those stocks have.

Five warning signs I would watch during the rest of earnings season

1. Stocks fall much further than options markets anticipated

Before earnings, options prices provide an indication of how much a stock might move following its announcement.

They do not predict direction, and the estimated range is not a hard boundary.

However, when a stock declines significantly more than the expected movement, it can indicate that investors are reassessing the company's prospects more aggressively than anticipated.

Alphabet, ServiceNow and Fortinet all exceeded their respective expected downside moves in the supplied October 28 snapshot.

One such event is not necessarily alarming for the broader market. Several occurring among influential companies deserve closer attention.

2. Initial earnings rallies fail to hold

This was an important observation in my earlier analysis of Netflix, Tesla and Meta's earnings reactions.

Meta and Tesla initially attracted buyers after reporting, only to see those gains disappear.

Microsoft now provides another test.

Its initial positive reaction suggests investors welcomed the results. But a stronger indication of sustained confidence would be a gain that survives the next regular trading session and subsequent reassessment.

The reverse applies to Alphabet. A substantial recovery from its initial decline would weaken the interpretation that investors are firmly rejecting its results.

3. Several important companies disappoint around the same time

A single company's disappointing earnings reaction may reflect something specific to that business.

For Alphabet, investors have been weighing search advertising performance and the cost of AI infrastructure expansion. For ServiceNow and Fortinet, software growth expectations and company-specific operating metrics have been important considerations.

These are different situations.

But if large companies across several industries repeatedly experience disappointing earnings reactions, investors should investigate whether the problem extends beyond individual businesses.

That could suggest weakening confidence in future earnings growth, demanding valuations or a broader reduction in risk appetite.

It would still be a hypothesis, not proof of a market-wide shift.

4. A small number of heavyweight stocks overwhelm improving participation

This is the warning I find especially useful for diversified stock investors.

Consider two portfolios.

One contains equal investments in 100 companies. The other allocates more money to companies with the largest market capitalizations.

Even if the same number of companies rise in both portfolios, the returns may differ substantially because of the amount invested in each company.

That is why I would monitor both the percentage of companies receiving positive earnings reactions and the capitalization-weighted performance of those reactions.

If breadth improves but the weighted results remain weak, the largest companies may still be a source of vulnerability.

5. The next trading session contradicts the initial reaction

After-hours price moves can be exaggerated by thinner liquidity, changing interpretations of conference calls and the arrival of new information.

A sharp overnight decline is meaningful, but it is not necessarily the final judgment.

For shorter-term traders, the first regular session can reveal whether buyers attempt to repair the damage or whether sellers continue to dominate.

For longer-term investors, several trading sessions, updated analyst expectations and management guidance may be more useful than the opening reaction alone.

The distinction matters because an immediate price shock is not the same thing as a sustained change in market expectations.

What could change the interpretation?

The October 29 session and subsequent earnings announcements should provide further evidence.

I would become more concerned if Alphabet, ServiceNow and Fortinet retain most of their initial losses, additional major companies experience downside moves beyond options expectations, and positive earnings reactions repeatedly fade.

A broader deterioration across different sectors would make the warning more significant.

Conversely, I would be encouraged if some of these sharp declines are repaired, Microsoft's positive reaction holds, and improving breadth begins translating into stronger capitalization-weighted results.

The next reporting group is particularly relevant. Amazon and Intel are scheduled to report after the October 29 close, while Eli Lilly and Mastercard are among the major companies reporting before the opening bell. These results can help determine whether the divergence remains concentrated in technology or extends elsewhere.

A warning sign, but not a confirmed bearish market

For now, I would resist concluding that this earnings season has turned decisively bearish.

There have been encouraging reactions, substantial business growth and companies reporting better-than-expected results. Microsoft's latest earnings illustrate that investors are still willing to reward performance they find convincing.

Nevertheless, the growing separation between winning and losing earnings reactions warrants attention.

Investors might be becoming increasingly selective, demanding stronger evidence that reported growth, future expectations and the capital required to deliver that growth are aligned.

The coming sessions should tell us more.

My conclusion is not that Wall Street has stopped rewarding strong companies. It is that some companies now appear to face a much higher bar for satisfying investors.

And when those companies are among the largest holdings in major stock-market indices, their earnings reactions matter well beyond their individual shareholders.

item.title: Google stock analysis after earnings: Is AI eating into search profits?
item.description:
Google’s AI may be cannibalizing search. Can Gemini pay the bill?

More AI usage does not guarantee more profit. Alphabet’s latest results sharpen a question for investors: can advertising and subscriptions replace the value of the searches AI absorbs?

Analysis | October 29, 2026 | Alphabet: GOOGL and GOOG

Google stock is getting hammered almost 11% in pre-market. For today, I'm watching $280-$284 for a dip. Temporary or not? I don't know but in any case, my hypothesis is that Google’s AI tools may be replacing some search advertising opportunities faster than new revenue streams can compensate. Alphabet’s latest earnings give that concern substance, but do not establish a net loss: Search revenue is still growing, and the company does not disclose enough Gemini economics to settle the question.

Perhaps like you, I’ve been clicking fewer links in Google search results over the past year. That change in my own habits has made me wonder: if more of us get what we need from an AI answer, what happens to the business built around the searches and clicks that follow?

The risk I see is that Google succeeds at changing how people find information, while weakening the economics that made its search business so valuable.

The latest earnings give my hypothesis something concrete

Alphabet’s results for the quarter ended September 30, released October 28, showed Google Search & other revenue rising 12% to $63.35 billion. Across Alphabet, revenue increased 25% to $127.6 billion. These are growth figures, not evidence of an outright collapse.

Markets were less impressed than the revenue growth alone suggests. As investingLive reported, Alphabet shares fell more than 9% after hours as the Search miss and cash burn overshadowed Cloud growth. That reaction reflects several concerns and should not be treated as proof of cannibalization.

What catches my attention, though, is management’s explanation of the slowdown.

On the earnings call, chief business officer Philipp Schindler said rapid growth in AI Mode queries had affected performance because AI Mode was monetizing at a lower level. He also identified foreign exchange as the largest driver of Search’s deceleration from the previous quarter, alongside changes in retail advertising and World Cup-related spending.

That distinction matters. AI was a contributor, not the sole explanation.

Meanwhile, CEO Sundar Pichai said Search query growth was its strongest in five years and the Gemini app had reached one billion users.

To me, those disclosures raise an important possibility: Google can generate more activity without generating the same revenue from each interaction.

They do not establish how much revenue would have existed without AI. Some AI questions may be entirely new demand. Others may replace traditional searches. Public disclosures do not cleanly separate the two.

Zero clicks for publishers does not mean zero revenue for Google

My own browsing habits are only one observation. There is broader evidence worth considering.

Pew Research Center studied browsing activity from 900 U.S. adults in March 2025. Users clicked a traditional result on 8% of visits to Google pages with an AI summary, compared with 15% without one. Links inside the summaries attracted clicks on just 1% of visits.

This was an observational study, not a randomized experiment or a measurement of Google’s advertising revenue. Search results were reconstructed in April, and queries that produce summaries differ from those that do not. It nevertheless provides evidence that reading an answer can replace visiting a website.

Three products also need separating: AI Overviews summarize information within search results; AI Mode provides conversational Search; Gemini is a separate assistant. Their revenue models need not be identical.

Google does not earn money whenever someone clicks an ordinary, unpaid search result. Losing a publisher referral therefore does not automatically cost Google a paid click. Ads can appear within or alongside AI Overviews and AI Mode.

The risk I am more interested in comes when one AI conversation replaces a sequence of commercially valuable searches.

A person researching a holiday might previously have searched repeatedly for destinations, hotels and comparisons. An assistant could compress that process into a shortlist. If fewer valuable advertising opportunities remain, and new placements do not compensate, Google loses potential revenue even while delivering a better experience.

Conversely, an assistant that helps someone reach a purchase faster could produce a more valuable advertising opportunity. The outcome depends on what users do next, not simply whether they leave Google.

Gemini subscriptions are not an automatic replacement

I would not assume that paid AI plans can simply replace whatever advertising revenue disappears.

The numbers are less straightforward.

Google lists AI Pro at $19.99 per month in the U.S., bundled with benefits beyond the Gemini assistant. That price is not equivalent to incremental Gemini profit. Existing subscribers may upgrade from another paid plan, promotions affect receipts, and serving their requests costs money.

Alphabet’s financial reporting does not provide a standalone Gemini consumer subscription revenue and profit figure. Its broader subscriptions, platforms and devices category mixes several businesses. Nor does one billion Gemini users mean one billion paying customers.

Let’s put some numbers around that question.

Suppose the annualized value of Search revenue lost relative to an otherwise achievable outcome equaled just 1% of its latest quarterly revenue run rate. Using $63.35 billion per quarter, that would be approximately $2.53 billion a year.

Replacing that gross revenue at $19.99 a month would require roughly 10.6 million additional subscribers paying for an entire year.

This is an illustration, not an estimate of actual cannibalization. It ignores discounts, churn, existing subscription spending and the cost of delivering AI. Replacing lost profit would require comparing the contribution margins of both businesses.

It also shows why subscriptions should not be dismissed. A sufficiently large, durable paying audience could make a meaningful difference.

The harder problem is converting enough users while keeping the free service attractive. A fixed monthly fee brings predictable revenue, but intensive usage can add costs without adding another subscription payment. Usage limits and higher-priced tiers can help, although they may also encourage price-sensitive users to look elsewhere.

Switching AI assistants may be easy. Rebuilding a working relationship may not be.

For someone asking occasional questions, moving to another AI platform can be as simple as opening a different app.

That creates a challenge for premium subscriptions. If several assistants answer everyday questions well enough, users can cancel, rotate subscriptions or use several free products.

Switching becomes harder when an assistant holds project history, understands preferences and connects to everyday work. An enterprise may also need to rebuild integrations, retest reliability and repeat security reviews.

My view is that the more durable advantage could come from how deeply an assistant fits into someone’s daily work. A temporary lead on a model benchmark may be easier for competitors to challenge.

But even that advantage is contestable.

Google already offers tools to import memories and chat histories from other AI services. Its documentation says project files, attachments and generated images do not transfer through the chat-history import.

This is evidence that switching friction can be reduced, not eliminated. A transferred conversation is not necessarily a functioning replacement for an established workflow.

There is an irony here: Google wants portability when it helps Gemini win customers. If comparable portability becomes widespread, it could also make Gemini customers easier to lose.

Cheaper, open AI could squeeze the subscription cushion

Open-weight models, whose trained parameters developers can obtain and deploy subject to their licenses, create another source of competitive pressure.

They can support lower-priced services, specialized assistants and some applications running on users’ own devices. Google participates in this market through Gemma, which it makes available for applications, hardware and hosted services.

The competitive threat does not require every open model to beat every premium model. For many routine tasks, being sufficiently useful at a lower price may be enough.

Stanford’s 2026 AI Index described convergence among leading models on one widely used evaluation, while also finding that the gap between the best closed and open models had widened again after previously narrowing. That is evidence of active competition, not proof that all models are interchangeable.

Nor does an open model guarantee a cheaper finished service. Hosting, security, maintenance, reliable information retrieval and customer support still cost money.

This is the potential squeeze that concerns me: AI could reduce some advertising opportunities while competition limits the subscription prices available to replace them.

Lower computing costs also help Google. They could make AI answers cheaper to deliver and improve margins even if customer prices fall.

Google could turn the threat into a stronger business

I also see a credible case for Google coming out of this stronger.

Google is developing commercial formats for AI Search, including conversational ads and offers linked to checkout. These are real product initiatives, although their long-term profitability remains unproven.

If an assistant understands what someone wants and helps complete the transaction, Google could capture value closer to the purchase. Fewer browsing steps would not necessarily mean less revenue.

Alphabet also has revenue sources beyond consumer subscriptions. Google Cloud revenue rose 103% to $30.7 billion in the latest quarter. Google Services operating income increased 17%, and its operating margin reached 40.7%.

Those figures challenge any claim that AI has already broken Alphabet’s operating model. Services includes more than Search, however, and shared AI research expenses also sit at the Alphabet level. The segment margin does not reveal Gemini’s standalone profitability.

Cash flow adds another complication. Alphabet reported negative quarterly free cash flow of $9.1 billion. Management attributed the pressure to capital spending, inventory for its chip systems business and a $5.2 billion European Commission fine payment. That cash outflow cannot simply be labeled a loss from AI search.

A related investor concern appears in investingLive’s report on Samsung’s share-price slide amid disappointment over the timing of shareholder returns. Samsung shares fell as much as 6.6% as investors awaited details of its broader return plan, due in late January, despite strong AI-related earnings.

Samsung’s situation does not establish a problem with Google’s search model. It illustrates a broader test for AI investments: how much cash reaches shareholders, and when? Strong demand and rising revenue do not settle that question on their own.

I also have to consider what happens if Google does not change. Preserving familiar Search economics temporarily could come at the cost of driving users toward competing assistants.

Internal cannibalization could be the cost of defending a business that would otherwise face external disruption.

Three paths I would consider as an investor

A profitable transition. AI generates new demand, advertising catches up, subscriptions retain customers and serving costs fall. Google protects its customer relationship and expands the ways it earns money from it.

A larger business with weaker economics. Usage keeps rising, but commercially valuable searches are partly replaced by less profitable interactions. Subscriptions and Cloud help, yet more investment is needed to generate each additional dollar of cash flow.

A shift in who controls the customer. Rival assistants become the starting point for research and purchases. Google may still supply models, computing or information behind the scenes, but another platform controls the recommendation and commercial relationship.

These are scenarios, not forecasts. Different parts of Alphabet could experience them simultaneously.

When assessing the next results, these are the questions I would focus on:

  • Does Search advertising growth strengthen after accounting for currency and comparison effects?
  • Does management provide evidence that AI advertising earns more per commercial task, alongside useful advertiser conversion data?
  • Do paid AI plans produce durable incremental revenue, rather than mainly trials, discounts or upgrades from existing subscriptions?
  • Do operating cash generation and investment spending move toward a more sustainable balance?
  • Are users becoming more committed to one assistant, or spreading their activity across interchangeable services?

Query counts alone cannot settle those questions. A long conversation may contain many prompts without representing many separate purchase opportunities.

My hypothesis remains: Google could remain a leader in AI while surrendering some of the exceptional economics of traditional search.

Gemini subscriptions may help close that gap. What I want to understand is whether they can do enough, alongside AI advertising and other businesses, to protect Google’s profitability. User growth alone does not answer that question. In terms of simplicity, IMHO, stock must, in the near future (till the end of Q1 2027) should reclaim back $310, in order to reignite the bullish case. That would be my line in the sand for Alphabet stock (ticker GOOG).

This article was written by Itai Levitan at investinglive.com.

item.title: HYPE token skyrockets as NYSE owner moves to bring Hyperliquid perpetual futures to US traders
item.description:
HYPE token is surging after Bloomberg reported that Intercontinental Exchange (ICE), the owner of the New York Stock Exchange, has joined forces with Trade.xyz to bring perpetual futures trading to US regulated markets using Hyperliquid’s blockchain infrastructure.

The proposed market would offer perpetual futures linked to equities, equity indexes, commodities and currencies. It would operate with its own clearing infrastructure, know-your-customer (KYC) procedures and anti-money-laundering (AML) controls, subject to regulatory approval. This represents a significant step toward bringing Hyperliquid’s onchain derivatives model into traditional US financial markets.

The partnership would significantly expand Hyperliquid’s addressable market. The platform has established itself as a major venue for onchain perpetual futures, including contracts tied to traditional assets such as oil, gold and equity indexes. Bringing these products into a regulated US framework would attract more institutional participants and additional trading volume.

Hyperliquid uses trading-fee revenue to fund purchases of its native token through its assistance fund. The proposed market should generate meaningful additional activity and contribute to the ecosystem’s economics, strengthening the bullish case for the HYPE token.

item.title: Bitcoin's $80,000 lifeline is looking rather fragile as tech stocks stumble
item.description:
So, just how many times can you actually poke the bear before it finally bites? Well, Bitcoin bulls might be on the verge of finding that out.

Because here we are again, with the cryptocurrency slipping back towards the key $80,000 level just as nerves around risk assets are starting to pick up once more. And while buyers have managed to hold the line so far, the feeble rebounds over the past week aren't exactly giving much reason for confidence.

It doesn't help that Wall Street is having another wobble of its own as fresh concerns over AI spending are weighing on tech stocks ahead of the open today. Meanwhile, the Fed hasn't exactly rolled out the red carpet for risk-taking either with their decision and Warsh's press conference yesterday.

And given Bitcoin's well-established sensitivity to broader risk sentiment, there is little reason to be surprised by its latest struggles. Having said that, there is a bigger concern here than just its correlation with tech stocks. The question for traders this week is how much longer can Bitcoin keep testing the $80,000 floor before buyers finally throw in the towel?

And the chart above captures that underlying tension quite nicely. Bitcoin is once again leaning on the $80,000 mark today and the repeated arrows near that level tell the story here.

Buyers have been trying to defend the key level but any bounce off it has hardly been convincing. As such, that makes this less of a successful hold of a major support level and more of a market that is nervously pacing around an important floor area.

For the time being at least, what stands out is that the bigger bullish structure is not broken yet. However, the upside momentum has clearly cooled after the run toward the $87,000 region in September and also earlier this month.

With that in mind, a break below $80,000 and one with more conviction could really expose plenty of vulnerabilities for Bitcoin next. The next deeper areas to watch look to be around the swing region closer to $76,000 and then the September lows just under the $75,000 level. After which, a stronger retreat towards $70,000 may very well come back into view.

As things stand, the bigger recovery structure is still intact; albeit barely. However, Bitcoin looks to be running out of room to keep testing buyers' patience.

Right now, the cryptocurrency is looking very much less like digital gold and more like a high-beta cousin of the Nasdaq. So as long as that remains true, then every wobble in the tech mood is going to keep crypto traders on edge.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.
